summary: Stable partitioning must classify the final linked-list node in the worst case, which makes linear time unavoidable. The current two-chain traversal inspects and relinks each node once and matches that bound.

optimality.argument: Consider two n-node lists that agree through their first n - 1 nodes but whose final node lies on opposite sides of x. Their stable partitioned outputs differ, so a correct algorithm must reach and inspect the final node to distinguish them, establishing an Omega(n) worst-case lower bound. The current algorithm advances monotonically through the list, detaches each node once, and appends it to one of two chains with constant pointer work, giving O(n) time.

replacement_checks.evidence: Changing only the final node from below x to at least x changes its required stable partition while leaving every earlier observation identical.
The current pointer visits each original node exactly once; detaching, classifying, appending, and the final chain join all take constant work per node.
The source-fidelity-verified examples cover interleaved partitions and a two-node reorder; black-box real-test execution verifies all existing ordinary checks without inspecting their definitions.
